entries.fbbde7e98126c70e148fdb343c7a1bf9f9d61d35: <div sID="gen33999" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Rev.4" sID="Rev.4"/> <div eID="gen33999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34000" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen34001" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the prophetical scene opens; and, as the epistolary part opened with a vision of Christ (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.1-Rev.1.20">ch. i.</reference>), so this part is introduced with a glorious appearance of the great God, whose throne is in heaven, compassed about with the heavenly host. This discovery was made to John, and in this chapter he, I. Records the heavenly sight he saw, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.1-Rev.4.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. And then, II. The heavenly songs he heard, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.8-Rev.4.11">ver. 8, to the end</reference>.
entries.d824e735bfdeabc11ea7b87af485255e3b633760: <div eID="gen34001" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen34000" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of Heaven. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 95.)</title> <div sID="gen34002" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> After this I looked, and, behold, a door <hi type="italic">was</hi> opened in heaven: and the first voice which I heard <hi type="italic">was</hi> as it were of a trumpet talking with me; which said, Come up hither, and I will show thee things which must be hereafter. <hi type="super">2</hi> And immediately I was in the spirit: and, behold, a throne was set in heaven, and <hi type="italic">one</hi> sat on the throne. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he that sat was to look upon like a jasper and a sardine stone: and <hi type="italic">there was</hi> a rainbow round about the throne, in sight like unto an emerald. <hi type="super">4</hi> And round about the throne <hi type="italic">were</hi> four and twenty seats: and upon the seats I saw four and twenty elders sitting, clothed in white raiment; and they had on their heads crowns of gold. <hi type="super">5</hi> And out of the throne proceeded lightnings and thunderings and voices: and <hi type="italic">there were</hi> seven lamps of fire burning before the throne, which are the seven Spirits of God. <hi type="super">6</hi> And before the throne <hi type="italic">there was</hi> a sea of glass like unto crystal: and in the midst of the throne, and round about the throne, <hi type="italic">were</hi> four beasts full of eyes before and behind. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the first beast <hi type="italic">was</hi> like a lion, and the second beast like a calf, and the third beast had a face as a man, and the fourth beast <hi type="italic">was</hi> like a flying eagle. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the four beasts had each of them six wings about <hi type="italic">him;</hi> and <hi type="italic">they were</hi> full of eyes within— <div eID="gen34002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34003" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of a second vision with which the apostle John was favoured: <hi type="italic">After this,</hi> that is, not only "after I had seen the vision of Christ walking in the midst of the golden candlesticks," but "after I had taken his messages from his mouth, and written and sent them to the several churches, according to his command, after this I had another vision." Those who well improve the discoveries they have had of God already are prepared thereby for more, and may expect them. Observe, <div eID="gen34003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34004" type="x-p"/> I. The preparation made for the apostle's having this vision. <div eID="gen34004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34005" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">A door was opened in heaven.</hi> Hence we learn, (1.) Whatever is transacted on earth is first designed and settled in heaven; there is the model of all the works of God; all of them are therefore before his eye, and he lets the inhabitants of heaven see as much of them as is fit for them. (2.) We can know nothing of future events but what God is pleased to discover to us; they are within the veil, till God opens the door. But, (3.) So far as God reveals his designs to us we may and ought to receive them, and not pretend to be wise above what is revealed. <div eID="gen34005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34006" type="x-p"/> 2. To prepare John for the vision, a trumpet was sounded, and he was called up into heaven, to have a sight there of the things which were to be hereafter. He was called into the third heavens. (1.) There is a way opened into the holiest of all, into which the sons of God may enter by faith and holy affections now, in their spirits when they die, and in their whole persons at the last day. (2.) We must not intrude into the secret of God's presence, but stay till we are called up to it. <div eID="gen34006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34007" type="x-p"/> 3. To prepare for this vision, <hi type="italic">the apostle was in the Spirit.</hi> He was in a rapture, as before (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.10">ch. i. 10</reference>), whether in the body or out of the body we cannot tell; perhaps he himself could not; however all bodily actions and sensations were for a time suspended, and his spirit was possessed with the spirit of prophecy, and wholly under a divine influence. The more we abstract ourselves from all corporeal things the more fit we are for communion with God; the body is a veil, a cloud, and clog to the mind in its transactions with God. We should as it were forget it when we go in before the Lord in duty, and be willing to drop it, that we may go up to him in heaven. This was the <hi type="italic">apparatus</hi> to the vision. Now observe, <div eID="gen34007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34008" type="x-p"/> II. The vision itself. It begins with the strange sights that the apostle saw, and they were such as these:— 1. He saw <hi type="italic">a throne set in heaven,</hi> the seat of honour, and authority, and judgment. Heaven is the throne of God; there he resides in glory, and thence he gives laws to the church and to the whole world, and all earthly thrones are under the jurisdiction of this throne that is set in heaven. 2. He saw a glorious one upon the throne. This throne was not empty; there was one in it who filled it, and that was God, who is here described by those things that are most pleasant and precious in our world: <hi type="italic">His countenance was like a jasper and a sardine-stone;</hi> he is not described by any human features, so as to be represented by an image, but only by his transcendent brightness. This jasper is a transparent stone, which yet offers to the eye a variety of the most vivid colours, signifying the glorious perfections of God; the sardine-stone is red, signifying the justice of God, that essential attribute of which he never divests himself in favour of any, but gloriously exerts it in the government of the world, and especially of the church, through our Lord Jesus Christ. This attribute is displayed in pardoning as well as in punishing, in saving as well as in destroying sinners. 3. He saw <hi type="italic">a rainbow about the throne, like unto an emerald,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.4.3">v. 3</reference>. The rainbow was the seal and token of the covenant of the providence that God made with Noah and his posterity with him, and is a fit emblem of that covenant of promise that God has made with Christ as the head of the church, and all his people in him, which covenant is as the waters of Noah unto God, an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things and sure. This rainbow looked like <hi type="italic">the emerald;</hi> the most prevailing colour was a pleasant green, to show the reviving and refreshing nature of the new covenant. 4. He saw <hi type="italic">four-and-twenty seats</hi> round about the throne, not empty, but filled with <hi type="italic">four-and-twenty elders,</hi> presbyters, representing, very probably, the whole church of God, both in the Old-Testament and in the New-Testament state; not the ministers of the church, but rather the representatives of the people. Their sitting denotes their honour, rest, and satisfaction; their sitting about the throne signifies their relation to God, their nearness to him, the sight and enjoyment they have of him. <hi type="italic">They are clothed in white raiment,</hi> the righteousness of the saints, both imputed and inherent; <hi type="italic">they had on their heads crowns of gold,</hi> signifying the honour and authority given them of God, and the glory they have with him. All these may in a lower sense be applied to the gospel church on earth, in its worshipping assemblies; and, in the higher sense, to the church triumphant in heaven. 5. He perceived lightnings and voices proceeding out of the throne; that is, the awful declarations that God makes to his church of his sovereign will and pleasure. Thus he gave forth the law on mount Sinai; and the gospel has not less glory and authority than the law, though it be of a more spiritual nature. 6. He saw <hi type="italic">seven lamps of fire burning before the throne,</hi> which are explained to be <hi type="italic">the seven Spirits of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.4.5">v. 5</reference>), the various gifts, graces, and operations of the Spirit of God in the churches of Christ; these are all dispensed according to the will and pleasure of him who sits upon the throne. 7. He saw <hi type="italic">before the throne a sea of glass, like unto crystal.</hi> As in the temple there was a great vessel of brass filled with water, in which the priests were to wash when they went to minister before the Lord (and this was called a <hi type="italic">sea</hi>), so in the gospel church the sea or laver for purification is the blood of the Lord Jesus Christ, who cleanses from all sin, even from sanctuary-sins. In this all those must be washed that are admitted into the gracious presence of God on earth or his glorious presence in heaven. 8. He saw <hi type="italic">four animals,</hi> living creatures, between the throne and the circle of elders (as seems most probable), standing between God and the people; these seem to signify the ministers of the gospel, not only because of this their situation nearer to God, and between him and the elders or representatives of the Christian people, and because fewer in number than the people, but as they are here described, (1.) By their many eyes, denoting sagacity, vigilance, and circumspection. (2.) By their lion-like courage, their great labour and diligence (in which they resemble the ox), their prudence and discretion becoming men, and their sublime affections and speculations, by which they mount up <hi type="italic">with wings like eagles towards heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.4.7">v. 7</reference>), and these wings full of eyes within, to show that in all their meditations and ministrations they are to act with knowledge, and especially should be well acquainted with themselves and the state of their own souls, and see their own concern in the great doctrines and duties of religion, watching over their own souls as well as the souls of the people. (3.) By their continual employment, and that is, praising God, and not ceasing to do so night and day. The elders sit and are ministered unto; these stand and minister: they rest not night nor day. This now leads to the other part of the representation.

entries.bb8a6d51896498f734bc71dc823587c55bd6fca1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19114"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Rev.4.1-Rev.4.11">Re 4:1-11</reference>. Vision of God's Throne in Heaven; the Four and Twenty Elders; the Four Living Creatures.</title> <div sID="gen41498" type="x-p"/> Here begins the Revelation proper; and first, the fourth and fifth chapters set before us the heavenly scenery of the succeeding visions, and God on His throne, as the covenant God of His Church, the Revealer of them to His apostle through Jesus Christ. The first great portion comprises the opening of the seals and the sounding of the trumpets (fourth to eleventh chapters). As the communication respecting the seven churches opened with a suitable vision of the Lord Jesus as Head of the Church, so the second part opens with a vision suitable to the matter to be revealed. The scene is changed from earth to heaven.<div eID="gen41498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41499" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19114"/><hi type="bold">1. After this--</hi>Greek, "After these things," marking the opening of the next vision in the succession. Here is the transition from "the things which are" (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.19">Re 1:19</reference>), the existing state of the seven churches, as a type of the Church in general, in John's time, to "the things which shall be hereafter," namely, in relation to the time when John wrote.<div eID="gen41499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41500" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I looked--</hi>rather as Greek, "I saw" in vision; not as English Version means, I directed my look that way.<div eID="gen41500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was--</hi>Omit, as not being in the Greek.<div eID="gen41501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">opened--</hi>"standing open"; not as though John saw it in the act of being opened. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.1">Eze 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.3.16">Mt 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.56">Ac 7:56</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.10.11">10:11</reference>. But in those visions the heavens opened, disclosing the visions to those below on earth. Whereas here, heaven, the temple of God, remains closed to those on earth, but John is transported in vision through an open door up into heaven, whence he can see things passing on earth or in heaven, according as the scenes of the several visions require.<div eID="gen41502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41503" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the first voice which I heard--</hi>the voice which I heard at first, namely, in <reference osisRef="Rev.1.10">Re 1:10</reference>; the former voice.<div eID="gen41503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41504" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was as it were--</hi>Omit was, it not being in the Greek. "Behold" governs in sense both "a door," &c., and "the first voice," &c.<div eID="gen41504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41505" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Come up hither--</hi>through the "open door."<div eID="gen41505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41506" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be--</hi>come to pass.<div eID="gen41506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hereafter--</hi>Greek, "after these things": after the present time (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.19">Re 1:19</reference>). <div eID="gen41507" type="x-p"/>
entries.9e7c0729b87438a047803cf86d16cbcb8fcdbcc9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19115"/><div sID="gen41508" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19115"/><hi type="bold">2. And--</hi>omitted in the two oldest manuscripts, Vulgate, Syriac.<div eID="gen41508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41509" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I was, &c.--</hi>Greek, "I became in the Spirit" (see on <reference osisRef="Rev.1.10">Re 1:10</reference>): I was completely rapt in vision into the heavenly world.<div eID="gen41509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41510" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was set--</hi>not was placed, but was situated, literally, "lay."<div eID="gen41510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one sat on the throne--</hi>the Eternal Father: the Creator (<reference osisRef="Rev.4.11">Re 4:11</reference>): also compare <reference osisRef="Rev.4.8">Re 4:8</reference> with <reference osisRef="Rev.1.4">Re 1:4</reference>, where also the Father is designated, "which is, and was, and is to come." When the Son, "the Lamb," is introduced, <reference osisRef="Rev.5.5-Rev.5.9">Re 5:5-9</reference>, a new song is sung which distinguishes the Sitter on the throne from the Lamb, "Thou hast redeemed us to God," and <reference osisRef="Rev.5.13">Re 5:13</reference>, "Unto Him that sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb." So also in <reference osisRef="Rev.5.7">Re 5:7</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Da 7:13</reference>, the Son of man brought before the Ancient of days is distinguished from Him. The Father in essence is invisible, but in Scripture at times is represented as assuming a visible form. <div eID="gen41511" type="x-p"/>
entries.ecc9bac29d2be61931e87bd45fdb89def26647e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19116"/><div sID="gen41512" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19116"/><hi type="bold">3. was--</hi>omitted in the two oldest manuscripts but supported by Vulgate and Coptic.<div eID="gen41512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41513" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to look upon--</hi>Greek, "in sight," or "appearance."<div eID="gen41513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">jasper--</hi>From <reference osisRef="Rev.21.11">Re 21:11</reference>, where it is called most precious, which the jasper was not, Ebrard infers it was a diamond. Ordinarily, the jasper is a stone of various wavy colors, somewhat transparent: in <reference osisRef="Rev.21.11">Re 21:11</reference> it represents watery crystalline brightness. The sardine, our cornelian, or else a fiery red. As the watery brightness represents God's holiness, so the fiery red His justice executing fiery wrath. The same union of white or watery brightness and fiery redness appears in <reference osisRef="Rev.1.14">Re 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.1">10:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.4">Eze 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.2">8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.9">Da 7:9</reference>.<div eID="gen41514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41515" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rainbow round about the throne--</hi>forming a complete circle (type of God's perfection and eternity: not a half circle as the earthly rainbow) surrounding the throne vertically. Its various colors, which combined form one pure solar ray, symbolize the varied aspects of God's providential dealings uniting in one harmonious whole. Here, however, the predominating color among the prismatic colors is green, the most refreshing of colors to look upon, and so symbolizing God's consolatory promises in Christ to His people amidst judgments on His foes. Moreover, the rainbow was the appointed token of God's covenant with all flesh, and His people in particular. Hereby God in type renewed to man the grant originally made to the first Adam. The antitype will be the "new heavens and the new earth" restored to redeemed man, just as the earth, after the destruction by the flood, was restored to Noah. As the rainbow was first reflected on the waters of the world's ruin, and continues to be seen only when a cloud is brought over the earth, so another deluge, namely, of fire, shall precede the new heavens and earth: the Lord, as here, on His throne, whence (<reference osisRef="Rev.4.5">Re 4:5</reference>) proceed "lightnings and thunderings," shall issue the commission to rid the earth of its oppressors: but then, amidst judgment, when other men's hearts fail them for fear, the believer shall be reassured by the rainbow, the covenant token, round the throne (compare De Burgh, Exposition of Revelation). The heavenly bow speaks of the shipwreck of the world through sin: it speaks also of calm and sunshine after the storm. The cloud is the regular token of God's and Christ's presence, for example, in the tabernacle's holiest place; on Mount Sinai at the giving of the law; at the ascension (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.9">Ac 1:9</reference>); at His coming again (<reference osisRef="Rev.4.7">Re 4:7</reference>). <div eID="gen41515" type="x-p"/>
entries.41282626871452ecf68f33182a9a72a9bb9bbe1a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19117"/><div sID="gen41516" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19117"/><hi type="bold">4. seats--</hi>rather as the Greek is translated in this very verse, "thrones," of course lower and smaller than the grand central throne. So <reference osisRef="Rev.16.10">Re 16:10</reference>, "the seat (rather, throne) of the beasts," in hellish parody of God's throne.<div eID="gen41516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41517" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">four and twenty elders--</hi>Greek, "the four and twenty (or as one oldest manuscript, 'twenty-four') elders": the well-known elders [Alford]. But Tregelles translates, "Upon the twenty-four thrones (I saw: omitted in two oldest manuscripts) elders sitting": which is more probable, as the twenty-four elders were not mentioned before, whereas the twenty-four thrones were. They are not angels, for they have white robes and crowns of victory, implying a conflict and endurance, "Thou hast redeemed us": they represent the Heads of the Old and New Testament churches respectively, the Twelve Patriarchs (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.7.5-Rev.7.8">Re 7:5-8</reference>, not in their personal, but in their representative character), and Twelve Apostles. So in <reference osisRef="Rev.15.3">Re 15:3</reference>, "the song of Moses, and of the Lamb," the double constituents of the Church are implied, the Old Testament and the New Testament. "Elders" is the very term for the ministry both of the Old and New Testament, the Jewish and the catholic Gentile Church. The tabernacle was a "pattern" of the heavenly antitype; the holy place, a figure of HEAVEN ITSELF. Thus Jehovah's throne is represented by the mercy seat in the holiest, the Shekinah-cloud over it. "The seven lamps of fire before the throne" (<reference osisRef="Rev.4.5">Re 4:5</reference>) are antitypical to the seven-branched candlestick also in the holiest, emblem of the manifold Spirit of God: "the sea of glass" (<reference osisRef="Rev.4.6">Re 4:6</reference>) corresponds to the molten sea before the sanctuary, wherein the priests washed themselves before entering on their holy service; so introduced here in connection with the redeemed "priests unto God" (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Rev.15.2">Re 15:2</reference>). The "four living creatures" (<reference osisRef="Rev.4.6">Re 4:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.7">7</reference>) answer to the cherubim over the mercy seat. So the twenty-four throned and crowned elders are typified by the twenty-four chiefs of the twenty-four courses of priests, "Governors of the sanctuary, and governors of God" (<reference osisRef="1Chr.24.5">1Ch 24:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.25.1-1Chr.25.31">25:1-31</reference>). <div eID="gen41517" type="x-p"/>
entries.063d334ff31c4a409ee71ef72a7950fbd5861d70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19118"/><div sID="gen41518" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19118"/><hi type="bold">5. proceeded--</hi>Greek, "proceed."<div eID="gen41518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41519" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thunderings and voices--</hi>The two oldest manuscripts transpose, "voices and thunderings." Compare at the giving of the law on Sinai, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.16">Ex 19:16</reference>. "The thunderings express God's threats against the ungodly: there are voices in the thunders (<reference osisRef="Rev.10.3">Re 10:3</reference>), that is, not only does He threaten generally, but also predicts special judgments" [Grotius].<div eID="gen41519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41520" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seven lamps ... seven Spirits--</hi>The Holy Spirit in His sevenfold operation, as the light-and-life Giver (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.5.6">Re 5:6</reference>, seven eyes ... the seven Spirits of God; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.4">Re 1:4</reference>; 21:23; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.105">Psa 119:105</reference>) and fiery purifier of the godly, and consumer of the ungodly (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.11">Mt 3:11</reference>). <div eID="gen41520" type="x-p"/>
entries.a953b5fc2600ce589574f0912bab048adbb9f216: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19119"/><div sID="gen41521" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19119"/>6. Two oldest manuscripts, A, B, Vulgate, Coptic, and Syriac read, "As it were a sea of glass."<div eID="gen41521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41522" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like ... crystal--</hi>not imperfectly transparent as the ancient common glass, but like rock crystal. Contrast the turbid "many waters" on which the harlot "sitteth" (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.1">Re 17:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.17.15">15</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Job.37.18">Job 37:18</reference>, "the sky ... as a molten looking-glass." Thus, primarily, the pure ether which separates God's throne from John, and from all things before it, may be meant, symbolizing the "purity, calmness, and majesty of God's rule" [Alford]. But see the analogue in the temple, the molten sea before the sanctuary (see on <reference osisRef="Rev.4.4">Re 4:4</reference>, above). There is in this sea depth and transparency, but not the fluidity and instability of the natural sea (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.21.1">Re 21:1</reference>). It stands solid, calm, and clear, God's judgments are called "a great deep" (<reference osisRef="Ps.36.6">Psa 36:6</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Rev.15.2">Re 15:2</reference> it is a "sea of glass mingled with fire." Thus there is symbolized here the purificatory baptism of water and the Spirit of all who are made "kings and priests unto God." In <reference osisRef="Rev.15.2">Re 15:2</reference> the baptism with the fire of trial is meant. Through both all the king-priests have to pass in coming to God: His judgments, which overwhelm the ungodly, they stand firmly upon, as on a solid sea of glass; able like Christ to walk on the sea, as though it were solid.<div eID="gen41522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41523" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">round about the throne--</hi>one in the midst of each side of the throne.<div eID="gen41523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41524" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">four beasts--</hi>The Greek for "beasts," <reference osisRef="Rev.13.1">Re 13:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.11">11</reference>, is different, therion, the symbol for the carnal man by opposition to God losing his true glory, as lord, under Him, of the lower creatures, and degraded to the level of the beast. Here it is zoon, "living creatures"; not beast. <div eID="gen41524" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa03d37fc64209389178b511ee7402d10dbdee19: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19120"/><div sID="gen41525" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19120"/><hi type="bold">7. calf--</hi>"a steer" [Alford]. The Septuagint often uses the Greek term here for an ox (<reference osisRef="Exod.22.1">Ex 22:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.29.10">29:10</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen41525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41526" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a man--</hi>The oldest manuscripts have "as of a man." <div eID="gen41526" type="x-p"/>
entries.a314ef1ea71cbb5e13e266921f27b5d5451c8097: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv19121"/><div sID="gen41527" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv19121"/><hi type="bold">8. about him--</hi>Greek, "round about him." Alford connects this with the following sentence: "All round and within (their wings) they are (so two oldest manuscripts, A, B, and Vulgate read) full of eyes." John's object is to show that the six wings in each did not interfere with that which he had before declared, namely, that they were "full of eyes before and behind." The eyes were round the outside of each wing, and up the inside of each when half expanded, and of the part of body in that inward recess.<div eID="gen41527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41528" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rest not--</hi>literally, "have no rest." How awfully different the reason why the worshippers of the beast "have no rest day nor night," namely, "their torment for ever and ever."<div eID="gen41528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41529" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Holy, holy, holy--</hi>The "tris-hagion" of the Greek liturgies. In <reference osisRef="Isa.6.3">Is 6:3</reference>, as here, it occurs; also <reference osisRef="Ps.99.3">Psa 99:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.9">5, 9</reference>, where He is praised as "holy," (1) on account of His majesty (<reference osisRef="Rev.4.1">Re 4:1</reference>) about to display itself; (2) His justice (<reference osisRef="Rev.4.4">Re 4:4</reference>) already displaying itself; (3) His mercy (<reference osisRef="Rev.4.6-Rev.4.8">Re 4:6-8</reference>) which displayed itself in times past. So here "Holy," as He "who was"; "Holy," as He "who is": "Holy," as He "who is to come." He showed Himself an object of holy worship in the past creation of all things: more fully He shows Himself so in governing all things: He will, in the highest degree, show Himself so in the consummation of all things. "Of (from) Him, through Him, and to Him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen." In <reference osisRef="Isa.6.3">Is 6:3</reference> there is added, "the whole EARTH is full of His glory." But in Revelation this is deferred until the glory of THE Lord fills the earth, His enemies having been destroyed [Bengel].<div eID="gen41529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41530" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Almighty--</hi>answering to "Lord of hosts" (Sabaoth), <reference osisRef="Isa.6.3">Is 6:3</reference>.<div eID="gen41530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen41531" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The cherubim here have six wings, like the seraphim in <reference osisRef="Isa.6.2">Is 6:2</reference>; whereas the cherubim in <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.6">Eze 1:6</reference> had four wings each. They are called by the same name, "living creatures." But whereas in Ezekiel each living creature has all four faces, here the four belong severally one to each. See on <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.6">Eze 1:6</reference>. The four living creatures answer by contrast to the four world powers represented by four beasts. The Fathers identified them with the four Gospels, Matthew the lion, Mark the ox, Luke the man, John the eagle: these symbols, thus viewed, express not the personal character of the Evangelists, but the manifold aspect of Christ in relation to the world (four being the number significant of world-wide extension, for example, the four quarters of the world) presented by them severally: the lion expressing royalty, as Matthew gives prominence to this feature of Christ; the ox, laborious endurance, Christ's prominent characteristic in Mark; man, brotherly sympathy with the whole race of man, Christ's prominent feature in Luke; the eagle, soaring majesty, prominent in John's description of Christ as the Divine Word. But here the context best suits the view which regards the four living creatures as representing the redeemed election-Church in its relation of ministering king-priests to God, and ministers of blessing to the redeemed earth, and the nations on it, and the animal creation, in which man stands at the head of all, the lion at the head of wild beasts, the ox at the head of tame beasts, the eagle at the head of birds and of the creatures of the waters. Compare <reference osisRef="Rev.5.8-Rev.5.10">Re 5:8-10</reference>, "Thou hast redeemed us by Thy blood out of every kindred ... and hast made us unto our God kings and priests: and we shall reign on the earth"; and <reference osisRef="Rev.20.4">Re 20:4</reference>, the partakers with Christ of the first resurrection, who conjointly with Him reign over the redeemed nations that are in the flesh. Compare as to the happy and willing subjection of the lower animal world, Is 11:6-8; 65:25; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.25">Eze 34:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.18">Ho 2:18</reference>. Jewish tradition says the "four standards" under which Israel encamped in the wilderness, to the east, Judah, to the north, Dan, to the west, Ephraim, to the south, Reuben, were respectively a lion, an eagle, an ox, and a man, while in the midst was the tabernacle containing the Shekinah symbol of the Divine Presence. Thus we have "the picture of that blessed period when--</hi>the earth having been fitted for being the kingdom of the Father--the court of heaven will be transferred to earth, and the 'tabernacle of God shall be with men' (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.3">Re 21:3</reference>), and the whole world will be subject to a never-ending theocracy" (compare De Burgh, Exposition of Revelation). The point of union between the two views given above is: Christ is the perfect realization of the ideal of man; Christ is presented in His fourfold aspect in the four Gospels respectively. The redeemed election-Church similarly, when in and through Christ (with whom she shall reign) she realizes the ideal of man, shall combine in herself human perfections having a fourfold aspect: (1) kingly righteousness with hatred of evil and judicial equity, answering to the "lion"; (2) laborious diligence in every duty, the "ox"; (3) human sympathy, the "man"; (4) the contemplation of heavenly truth, the "eagle." As the high-soaring intelligence, the eagle, forms the contrasted complement to practical labor, the ox bound to the soil; so holy judicial vengeance against evil, the lion springing suddenly and terribly on the doomed, forms the contrasted complement to human sympathy, the man. In <reference osisRef="Isa.6.2">Is 6:2</reference> we read, "Each had six wings: with twain he covered his face (in reverence, as not presuming to lift up his face to God), with twain he covered his feet (in humility, as not worthy to stand in God's holy presence), and with twain he did fly [in obedient readiness to do instantly God's command]." <div eID="gen41531" type="x-p"/>

entries.5c26575ca5b4de822b79f35d2b89d0032a2fdd89: <div eID="gen55969" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen55970" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen55971" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen55971" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen55970" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen55972" type="x-p"/> John sees the throne of God in heaven surrounded by twenty-four elders; and four living creatures, full of eyes; which all join in giving glory to the Almighty, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.1-Rev.4.11">Rev 4:1-11</reference>. <div eID="gen55972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55973" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen55973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55974" type="x-p"/> A door was opened in heaven - This appears to have been a visible aperture in the sky over his head.
entries.13bc37217ca7eee4373ef96a983c3016cf7d8373: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen55974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55975" type="x-p"/> I was in the Spirit - Rapt up in an ecstasy.
entries.eded4b660b75246f16b0c1ee710e85623f6cd606: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen55975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55976" type="x-p"/> And he that sat - There is here no description of the Divine Being, so as to point out any similitude, shape, or dimensions. entries.d7915d7ab9f59a4b37cae6d1242823837be5a4e1: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen55976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55977" type="x-p"/> Four and twenty elders - Perhaps this is in reference to the smaller Sanhedrin at Jerusalem, which was composed of twenty-three elders; or to the princes of the twenty-four courses of the Jewish priests which ministered at the tabernacle and the temple, at first appointed by David. <div eID="gen55977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55978" type="x-p"/> Clothed in white raiment - The garments of the priests. <div eID="gen55978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55979" type="x-p"/> On their heads crowns of gold - An emblem of their dignity. The Jewish writers represent human souls as being created first; and before they enter the body, each is taken by an angel into paradise, where it sees the righteous sitting in glory with crowns upon their heads. Rab. Tanchum, fol. 39, 4.
entries.cad95ae80af8001f7d6ac2416864d169c2377dd5: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen55979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55980" type="x-p"/> Seven lamps of fire - Seven angels, the attendants and ministers of the supreme King. See <reference osisRef="Rev.1.4">Rev 1:4</reference>, and the note there.
entries.ed45e9c79b03de8554cd33a0143c709822935389: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen55980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55981" type="x-p"/> Four beasts - Τεσσαρα ζωα· Four living creatures or four animals.
